answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence appears in Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969), the book that collected Bukowski’s underground newspaper column — Wikiquote files it under that work ↗, and a moderator at the Bukowski Forum located it on p. 161 of his Virgin paperback ↗. What is not right is the shorter “hard way / simple way” version the quote sites print.

source.excerpt: an intellectual is a man who says a simple thing in a difficult way; an artist is a man who says a difficult thing in a simple way.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ prints the sentence word for word inside its “Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969)” section — a work section, not the unsourced pile at the foot of the page.

A reader asked the Bukowski Forum ↗ to source the line in 2009 and got only guesses. In 2016 a moderator reopened the thread, gave the original wording, and named the book and page from his own Virgin paperback.
Goodreads’ page of quotations from the book ↗ carries the same lower-case wording under the same title, independently of the forum.
A search of Quote Investigator ↗ returns nothing on this line, and no competing author was found claiming it — the dispute here is over wording, not authorship.
source.excerptNote: Given as Wikiquote and Goodreads reproduce it, in Bukowski’s lower case and as a single semicolon-hinged sentence. The capitalised, two-sentence version that circulates online is a later tidy-up.

author.name: Charles Bukowski
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1920–1994 · German-born American poet, novelist and underground columnist
author.bio: Born in Andernach, Germany in 1920 and raised in Los Angeles, Bukowski spent most of his working life sorting mail for the US Post Office before quitting in 1969 to write full time on an offer from Black Sparrow Press. From 1967 he wrote a weekly column called Notes of a Dirty Old Man for the LA underground paper Open City — loose, drunk, funny prose that swerved without warning into flat statements like this one. He published poems, stories and six novels, and died in Los Angeles in 1994.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The wording usually isn’t.
misattribution.intro: For once the famous name checks out — this really is Bukowski, and it really is in a book. The trouble is that the version doing the rounds has been quietly rewritten, and for years nobody could say which book it came from.

items.who: “An intellectual says a simple thing in a hard way. An artist says a hard thing in a simple way.”
items.why: This compressed form is what the aggregators carry — AZQuotes prints it with no book cited at all ↗, and Goodreads carries it as a bare, unsourced attribution ↗. Bukowski’s printed sentence is longer, hinged on a semicolon, and says “difficult,” not “hard.”

items.who: The Captain Is Out to Lunch and the Sailors Have Taken Over the Ship
items.why: The first guess when the question was raised on the Bukowski Forum in 2009 ↗. The member who suggested it went back through the book, could not find the line, and reported finding only a passage developing the same idea. The thread sat unanswered until 2016.

Several near-identical sentences circulate as though they were this quote — “genius” in place of “artist,” “profound” in place of “difficult.” Those are separately documented Bukowski restatements ↗ from interviews and Hot Water Music, not this sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution holds: Wikiquote places the full sentence inside Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969) ↗. It is the semicolon, the lower case and the word “difficult” that get lost in transit.

context.heading: An aphorism that keeps getting simplified
lead: Bukowski was writing a weekly column for Open City, a Los Angeles underground paper, from 1967 until the paper folded; Essex House gathered the columns into Notes of a Dirty Old Man in 1969, and City Lights has published the book since 1973. The line arrives in that setting — not as literary theory, but as one flat sentence dropped into pages of bar talk and bad weekends.

He clearly liked the thought, because he kept coming back to it. Bukowski Forum members have collected several restatements ↗, including a version in the story “How to get published” in Hot Water Music and two in interviews reprinted in Sunlight Here I Am, where the subject shifts from the artist to the genius.
detailsBody: The irony is hard to miss. The version that dominates search results — “An intellectual says a simple thing in a hard way. An artist says a hard thing in a simple way.” — is tighter, more quotable, and not what he printed. Someone did to the sentence exactly what the sentence recommends, and then kept his name on it.
Bukowski’s own text runs as one sentence hinged on a semicolon, in lower case, with “is a man who” in both halves. If you are quoting him rather than quoting the internet, that is the form to use.
context.pull: A sentence about saying difficult things simply, steadily simplified in transit.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the exact sentence under a section headed "Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969)", and gives Bukowski's dates as 1920-1994.

A Bukowski Forum moderator (post #4, 27 Aug 2016) gives the original wording as "an intellectual is a man who says a simple thing in a difficult way; an artist is a man who says a difficult thing in a simple way" and states it was taken from Notes of a Dirty Old Man, page 161 in the Virgin edition; the thread was opened 5 Jun 2009 asking for a source, and an early reply guessed The Captain Is Out to Lunch and the Sailors Have Taken Over the Ship, then reported failing to find the line there.

A separate Bukowski Forum thread collects variations of the idea, including "I think genius is the ability to say difficult things in a simple way" (interview, reprinted in Sunlight Here I Am), "Genius might be the ability to say a profound thing in a simple way" from "How to get published" in Hot Water Music, and the Notes of a Dirty Old Man line.
Goodreads' quotations page for Notes of a Dirty Old Man carries the sentence in lower case, attributed to Charles Bukowski and that book.
Goodreads carries the compressed variant "An intellectual says a simple thing in a hard way. An artist says a hard thing in a simple way." attributed to Bukowski with no book or source specified.

AZQuotes prints the compressed variant "An intellectual says a simple thing in a hard way. An artist says a hard thing in a simple way." attributed to Charles Bukowski with no book or source citation.
Notes of a Dirty Old Man was published by Essex House in 1969, collecting Bukowski's underground newspaper columns, and City Lights now publishes the series.

Charles Bukowski was born 16 August 1920 in Andernach, Germany, died 9 March 1994 in Los Angeles, and from 1967 wrote the column Notes of a Dirty Old Man for the LA underground paper Open City; in 1969 he left the Post Office to write full time for Black Sparrow Press.
The Internet Archive holds a City Lights Books edition of Notes of a Dirty Old Man, San Francisco, 1973; the item is access-restricted, so its full text is not searchable.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation: a site search for "difficult thing in a simple way" returns Nothing Found.
